title: The Custom Die
primary_metric: square inches of cardboard net per cubic inch of product actually shipped, tooling-amortized

options.A: Approve The Standard Box -- a simple rectangular-prism box, cheap die, wasted space around every slice
options.B: Approve The Fitted Wedge -- a triangular-prism box fitted to the slice's real shape, pricier die, almost no wasted space

sources.claim: Price of a 24 in x 36 in, 200 lb test single-wall corrugated cardboard pad, at the 50-pad bundle-quantity price tier
sources.units: USD per individual pad (the supplier's own "PRICE PER PAD" column at its 50-pad tier; a 50-pad bundle costs $2.37 x 50 = $118.50, not $2.37 total)
sources.title: 24 x 36" 200 lb Cardboard Corrugated Pads -- White (product S-15058)
sources.note: Primary retailer's own current, dated-by-access price for a real, specified corrugated product (200 lb test, single-wall, 24x36 in). Used as the material-cost basis for both box options -- same raw stock, different net shapes cut from it. Derived figure used in-case: $2.37 / 864 sq in = $0.0027431/sq in. Re-verified 2026-09-06 (Tier 2 Probe 6, browser fetch of the live product page): the price at this SKU's 50-pad tier had moved from $2.24 (recorded 2026-09-05) to $2.37 -- a live retailer's SKU-level price is not fixed, and re-checking it is exactly what P6 exists to catch. All figures in this case were re-derived against the current $2.37 value; see RESEARCH_LOG.md.

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC section 4
concept_sheet: cases/_concepts/CONCEPTS_life-skills-first10_2026-09-03.md -- The Custom Die (approved concept, provided directly)

deliverables.text: A shape audit of all six whiteboard candidates: correctly name each 3-D shape from its description, and state why it does or does not make sense for The Wedge's triangular cross-section.
A dimensioned net of Option A and of Option B, built to scale, every face labeled, with each box's Length, Width, and Depth marked directly on the net.
A net-area material table: total square inches of cardboard each option's net uses, computed from the labeled nets in D2, not from either box's volume.
A wasted-space table: The Wedge's own volume vs. each box option's interior volume, and the wasted cubic inches / percent for each.

A tooling-amortized cost comparison: D3's net area plus each option's die cost spread across the expected order volume, expressed as square inches of cardboard per cubic inch of Wedge shipped; state the winner and margin.

balance.argument_a: The Standard Box's net uses 102.375 sq in of cardboard against a cheap $450 die (MA1); amortized across the expected 12,000-unit order volume (MA3) that works out to an effective 116.05 sq in per unit, or 4.298 sq in of cardboard per cubic inch of Wedge actually shipped -- the winning number at this volume even though the box wastes 59.1% of its interior space on every single order.
balance.argument_b: The Fitted Wedge's net uses only 79.91 sq in of cardboard -- 22% less material than Option A -- and wastes only 18.2% of its interior space instead of 59.1%. That real, sourced-material win is genuine and independent of any assumption. It only stops being the deciding factor because its $1,450 die (MA2) is more than 3x Option A's, and at only 12,000 units of amortization (MA3) that tooling gap outweighs the material savings by 6.39%.
balance.margin_basis: Net surface area (Appendix D-priced) plus each option's die cost converted to an equivalent cardboard quantity and spread across the expected order volume (Appendix E), divided by The Wedge's fixed 27 cubic inches, computed in cases/the-custom-die/sensitivity_model.py evaluate().

derived._note: Computed by cases/the-custom-die/sensitivity_model.py. case-readiness should re-derive independently. Re-derived 2026-09-06 after Appendix D's Uline price re-verification (P6) moved from $2.24 to $2.37/sheet -- see RESEARCH_LOG.md.
derived.twist_rejected_reading_note: 40,000 units/year converted DOWN into the original 8-week window (40000 * 8/52 = 6153.85, rounded 6,154) -- the reading Appendix E's horizon rule explicitly rejects (see MA3 basis and FACILITATOR.md Twist section). Under this rejected reading the verdict does NOT flip; Option A wins by an even larger margin (22.18%) than the base case, which is why the horizon rule had to be stated explicitly rather than left implicit.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: One-time steel-rule die cost, Option A (simple rectangular net, six straight panels, all 90-degree folds)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Industry pricing pages consistently describe die cost as scaling with rule footage and complexity, but published dollar figures vary widely across sources with no single primary methodology. This case fixes a representative value for the simplest possible die style -- one continuous run of straight cutting/creasing rule, no angled cuts.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The margin is sensitive to this value. Flexed +/-50% in Tier 2 probe 5.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: One-time steel-rule die cost, Option B (triangular-prism net, two triangular panels plus three angled rectangular panels)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Same sourcing limitation as MA1. This case fixes a value roughly 3.2x MA1's, reflecting the additional rule footage from the angled triangular panels and the extra setup a non-90-degree fold pattern requires, consistent with the qualitative pattern found across industry sources even though no source gave a defensible exact multiplier.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The margin is sensitive to this value. Flexed +/-50% in Tier 2 probe 5.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Expected order volume for The Wedge before the next re-tooling decision point
modeling_assumptions.basis: Tied to the bakery's own current nationwide order volume (see Background) -- the packaging team's working forecast that The Wedge accounts for roughly one week's worth of the bakery's present order volume before the next production run reaches a point where a die change could be considered again. The re-tooling horizon is explicitly defined in Appendix E as whatever order volume the team can confidently count on at decision time -- for an unproven product with no purchase commitment, that is only the near-term production window; if a buyer signs a purchase order guaranteeing a specific volume over a stated term, the confidently-known volume becomes the full guaranteed volume over that term, not a rate converted back into the shorter window. This closes the ambiguity Tier 2 Probe 4 originally found in the Twist (see QA_REPORT.md).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The margin is highly sensitive to this value and the verdict itself flips above approximately 16,230 units. Flexed +/-50% in Tier 2 probe 5; also the value the Twist directly revises.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: This is a genuine future demand forecast for a brand-new product at a company mid-hypergrowth; the true order volume before the next re-tooling decision cannot be known in advance by any amount of research. The case's own Twist deliberately revises this exact number once a real signed contract replaces the forecast, which is the mechanism, not a flaw.

A specific company's die-shop quote for one specific box shape is proprietary and never publicly indexed anywhere. MA2's $1,450 is a documented good-faith estimate anchored to the general complexity-scaling pattern (more rule footage and angled panels cost more) found consistently across multiple industry sources during research -- see RESEARCH_LOG.md -- not a real citation for this exact die.

sensitivity_note: The verdict is genuinely fragile to Appendix E's order-volume assumption (MA3): the crossover point where the two options tie is approximately 16,230 units, well within plausible range of this bakery's own stated growth. Flexing MA3 is expected to flip the winner; this is disclosed rather than hidden, consistent with SPEC section 6 and MCS-26.
